source_text: Quanto opusculum profligatur, breuiter iam retractanda sunt quae rursus occurrunt, quaedam uero et tramittenda, quae saepius occurrerunt. piget de lege adhuc congredi, qui totiens probauerim concessionem eius nullum argumentum praestare diuersi dei in Christo, praedicatam scilicet et repromissam in Christum apud creatorem, quatenus et ipsa (ista) epistola legem plurimum uidetur excludere. sed et iudicem deum ab apostolo circumferri saepe iam ostendimus et in iudice ultorem et creatorem in ultore. itaque et hic, cum dicit: non enim me pudet euangelii; uirtus enim dei est in salutem omni credenti, Iudaeo et Graeco, quia iustitia dei in eo reuelatur ex fide in fidem, sine dubio et euangelium et salutem iusto deo deputat, non bono, — ut ita dixerim secundum haeretici distinctionem — transferenti ex fide legis in fidem euangelii, suae utique legis et sui euangelii, quoniam et iram (dei) dicit reuelari de caelo super impietatem et iniustitiam hominum, qui ueritatem (in) iniustitia detineant. cuius dei ira? utique creatoris. ergo et ueritas eius erit, cuius et ira, quae reuelari habet in ultionem ueritatis. etiam adiciens: scimus autem iudicium dei secundum ueritatem esse et iram ipsam probauit, ex qua uenit iudicium pro ueritate, et ueritatem rursus eiusdem dei confirmauit, cuius iram probauit probando iudicium. aliud est, si ueritatem dei alterius in iniustitia detentam creator iratus ulciscitur. quantas autem foueas in ista uel maxime epistola Marcion fecerit auferendo quae uoluit, de nostri instrumenti integritate parebit. mihi sufficit, quae proinde eradenda non uidit quasi neglegentias et caecitates eius accipere. si enim iudicabit deus occulta hominum, tam eorum qui in lege deliquerunt quam eorum qui sine lege, — quia et hi (etsi) legem ignorant, at natura faciunt quae sunt legis — utique is deus iudicabit, cuius sunt et lex et ipsa natura, quae legis est instar ignorantibus legem. iudicabit autem quomodo? secundum euangelium, inquit, per Christum. ergo et euangelium et Christus illius sunt, cuius et lex et natura, quae per euangelium et Christum uindicabuntur a deo illo iudicio, de quo et supra: secundum ueritatem. ergo qua (ad) defendenda (ea) reueletur de caelo ira non nisi a deo irae, ita et hic sensus, pristino cohaerens, in quo iudicium creatoris edicitur, non potest in alium deum referri, qui nec iudicat nec irascitur, sed in illum, cuius dum haec sunt, iudicium dico et iram, etiam illa ipsius sint necesse est, per quae haec habent transigi, euangelium et Christus. et ideo uehitur in transgressores legis docentes non furari et furantes, ut homo dei legis, non ut creatorem ipsum his modis tangens, qui et furari uetans fraudem mandauerit in Aegyptios auri et argenti, quemadmodum et cetera in illum retorquent. scilicet apostolus uerebatur conuicium deo palam facere, a quo non uerebatur diuertisse. adeo autem Iudaeos incesserat, ut ingesserit propheticam increpationem: propter uos nomen dei blasphematur. quam ergo peruersum, ut ipse blasphemaret eum, cuius blasphemandi causa malos exprobrat! Praefert et circumcisionem cordis praeputi. atenim apud deum legis est facta circumcisio cordis, non carnis, spiritu, non littera. quodsi haec est circumcisio Hieremiae - et circumcidemini praeputia cordis - sicut et Moysei - et circumcidemini duricordiam uestram —, eius erit spiritus circumcidens cor, cuius et littera metens carnem, eius et Iudaeus, qui in occulto, cuius et Iudaeus in aperto, quia nec Iudaeum nominare uellet apostolus non Iudaeorum dei seruum. Tunc lex, nunc iustitia dei per fidem Christi. quae est ista distinctio? seruiuit deus tuus dispositioni creatoris, dans ei tempus et legi eius? an eius tunc, cuius et nunc? eius lex cuius et fides Christi? distinctio dispositionum est, non deorum. Monet iustificatos ex fide Christi. non ex lege, pacem ad deum habere. ad quem? cuius numquam fuimus hostes an cuius legi et naturae rebellauimus? nam si in eum competit pax, cum quo fuit bellum. ei et iustificabimur; et eius erit Christus, ex cuius fide iustificabimur, ad cuius pacem competit redigi hostes eius aliquando. Lex aut em, inquit, subintroiuit, ut abundaret delictum. quare? ut superabundaret, inquit, gratia. cuius dei gratia, si non cuius et lex? nisi si creator ideo legem intercalauit, ut negotium procuraret gratiae dei alterius et quidem aemuli, ne dixerim ignoti, ut, quemadmodum apud ipsum regnauerat peccatum in mortem, ita et gratia regnaret in iustitia in uitam per Iesum Christum (apud) aduersarium ipsius. propter hoc omnia concluserat lex creatoris sub delictum et totum mundum deduxerat in reatum et omne os obstruxerat, ne qui gloriaretur per illam, ut gratia seruaretur in gloriam Christi non creatoris, sed Marcionis ! Possum et hic de substantia Christi praestruere ex prospectu quaestionis subsecuturae. mortuos enim nos inquit legi (per corpus Christi.) ergo corpus Christi est. \'potest corpus contendi, non statim caro! sed et quaecumque substantia sit, cum eius nominat corpus, quem subicit ex mortuis resurrexisse, non potest aliud corpus intellegi quam carnis, in quam lex mortis est dicta. Ecce autem et testimonium perhibet legi et causa delicti eam excusat: quid ergo dicemus? quia lex peccaturn? absit! - eru. besce, Marcion, [absit] abominanti apostolo criminationem legissed ego delictum non scio nisi per legem. o summum ex hoc praeconium legis, per quam (non) licuit delictum latere! non ergo lex seduxit, sed peccatum per praecepti occasionem. quid deo imputas legis quod legi eius apostolus imputare non audet? atquin et adcumulat: lex sancta et praeceptum eius iustum et bonum. si taliter ueneratur legem creatoris, quomodo ipsum destruat nescio. quis discernit duos deos, iustum alium bonum alium, cum is utrumque debeat credi, cuius praeceptum et bonum et iustum est? si autem et spiritalem confirmat legem, utique et propheticam, utique et figuratam. debeo enim et hinc constituere Christum in lege figurate praedicatum, quo et a Iudaeis omnibus potuerit agnosci.
thought_title: Against Marcion's View of God and Law
pass_a_gloss: To what extent the little work is being destroyed, now briefly the things which occur again must be retraced, and certain things which have occurred more frequently must also be passed over. It wearies me to still contend about the law, I who have so many times proven that its concession provides no argument for a different God in Christ, namely the one preached and promised in Christ to the Creator, insofar as this very epistle seems to exclude the law for the most part. But we have also shown many times that God is being carried around as judge by the apostle, and in the judge, the avenger and the Creator are in the avenger. And so, even here, when he says: For I am not ashamed of the gospel; for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew and to the Greek, because the justice of God is revealed in it from faith to faith, undoubtedly both the gospel and salvation are attributed to the just God, not the good one, -- so to speak, according to the heretic's distinction -- transferring from the faith of the law to the faith of the gospel, certainly of His own law and His own gospel, since He also says that the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against the impiety and injustice of men, who detain the truth in injustice. Whose wrath is it? Certainly the Creator's. Therefore, the truth will also be His, whose wrath it is, which is to be revealed for the vindication of the truth. Also, adding: We know that the judgment of God is according to truth and He has also approved His wrath, from which judgment comes for the truth, and He has confirmed the truth of the same God, whose wrath He has approved by approving the judgment. It would be different if the truth of another God, detained in injustice, were being avenged by the angry Creator. But how many ditches Marcion has made in this epistle, or rather in the greatest epistle, by removing what he wanted, will be evident from the integrity of our instrument. It is enough for me that he did not see fit to eradicate what I have taken as his negligence and blindness. For if God will judge the hidden things of men, both of those who have transgressed the law and of those who are without the law, -- because these, even if they do not know the law, do by nature what the law does -- certainly that God will judge, whose law and nature it is, which is a likeness of the law for those who do not know the law. And how will He judge? According to the gospel, He says, through Christ. Therefore, both the gospel and Christ are of the same God, whose law and nature will be vindicated by God through the gospel and Christ, in that judgment about which it is said above: according to truth. Therefore, just as the wrath which is revealed from heaven is not except from the God of wrath, so also this sense, cohering with the previous one, in which the judgment of the Creator is proclaimed, cannot be referred to another God, who neither judges nor becomes angry, but to the one whose judgment and wrath these things are, and necessarily also the gospel and Christ, through which these things are transacted. And therefore, He is carried away against the transgressors of the law, teaching not to steal and stealing, as a man of God's law, not as the Creator Himself being touched in these ways, who, forbidding stealing, commanded fraud against the Egyptians with gold and silver, just as the other things are also turned against Him. Evidently, the apostle was afraid to make a public reproach to God, from whom he was not afraid to divert. And yet he had so reproached the Jews that he inserted a prophetic rebuke: Because of you the name of God is blasphemed. How perverse, therefore, that he himself would blaspheme the one whose blasphemy he reproaches the wicked for! He also prefers the circumcision of the heart to that of the flesh. But with God, the circumcision of the heart, not of the flesh, has been made, by the Spirit, not by the letter. Which, if this is the circumcision of Jeremiah -- and circumcise the foreskins of your hearts -- and of Moses -- and circumcise your hardened heart --, the Spirit circumcising the heart will be of the same God, whose letter cuts the flesh, and whose Jew, both the one in secret and the one in public, because the apostle would not have wanted to name the God of the Jews. Then the law, now the justice of God through the faith of Christ. What is this distinction? Has your God served the disposition of the Creator, giving Him time and His law? Or whose then, and whose now? Whose law, and whose faith of Christ? The distinction is of dispositions, not of gods. He warns those justified by the faith of Christ to have peace with God. With which God? The one whose we were never enemies, or the one whose law and nature we have rebelled against? For if peace is offered to the one with whom there was war, we will be justified to Him; and His will be Christ, through whose faith we will be justified, to whose peace it is fitting that His enemies be reduced. The law, he says, entered in, that sin might abound. Why? That grace might abound, he says. Whose God's grace, if not whose law also? Unless the Creator interposed the law so that He might provide a occasion for the grace of another God, and indeed a rival, lest I say an unknown one, so that just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign in justice in life through Jesus Christ, with the adversary Himself. For this reason, the Creator's law had concluded all things under sin and led the whole world into debt and stopped every mouth, so that no one might glory through it, so that the grace might be preserved for the glory of Christ, not the Creator's, but Marcion's! I can also establish here the substance of Christ from the prospect of the following question. For he says: We are dead to the law through the body of Christ. Therefore, Christ has a body. The body can be contended, not immediately flesh! But whatever substance it is, since he names it body, which he subjects to have risen from the dead, no other body can be understood except that of flesh, in which the law of death is spoken. Behold, however, he also bears witness to the law and excuses its cause: what then shall we say? That the law is sinful? Away with it! -- I abhor, Marcion, [away with it], the apostle abominating the accusation of the law, I do not know sin except through the law. O greatest praise of the law from this, that sin was not allowed to hide through it! Therefore, it is not the law that has deceived, but sin through the occasion of the command. What do you impute to God's law, which the apostle does not dare to impute? And yet he also accumulates: The law is holy and its commandment is just and good. If he venerates the law of the Creator in such a way, I do not know how he destroys it. Who distinguishes two gods, one just and the other good, when it is necessary to believe that the commandment of the one God is both good and just? But if he also confirms the spiritual law, certainly the prophetic one, certainly the figurative one. I ought to establish Christ, therefore, as having been predicted in the law in figure, so that He might be recognized by all the Jews.

pass_b_english: Since the pamphlet is being dismantled, I must briefly revisit the arguments that crop up again and simply pass over those that have surfaced repeatedly. I am sick of still contending about the law; I have proved time and again that its concession supplies no argument for a different God in Christ — specifically, the Christ preached and promised to the Creator — especially since this very epistle appears to exclude the law almost entirely. Yet we have also shown repeatedly that the apostle carries God around as judge, and in that judge the avenger and the Creator are one in the avenger.

So here too, when he says, "For I am not ashamed of the gospel; it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, Jew and Greek alike, because the justice of God is revealed in it from faith to faith" (Rom 1:16-17), he undoubtedly assigns both gospel and salvation to the just God, not the "good" one — to put it in the heretic's own terms — transferring from the faith of the law to the faith of the gospel, His own law and His own gospel, since he also declares that the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against the impiety and injustice of men who suppress the truth in injustice. Whose wrath? The Creator's, of course. Therefore the truth also belongs to the One whose wrath it is, a wrath slated to be revealed for the vindication of that truth.

He adds: "We know that the judgment of God is according to truth" (Rom 2:2), and he has validated that wrath, from which judgment comes for the truth, and he has confirmed the truth of the same God whose wrath he validated by validating the judgment. It would be a different matter if the Creator in anger were avenging the truth of another God suppressed in injustice. But the ditches Marcion has dug in this epistle — rather, the supreme epistle — by cutting out whatever he pleased, will be exposed by the integrity of our text. It suffices for me that he did not see fit to excise the passages I cite as evidence of his negligence and blindness.

If God judges the hidden things of men — both those who sinned under the law and those who sinned without it — since even the latter, though ignorant of the law, do by nature what the law requires, then that God will judge whose law and nature they are, a nature that serves as a likeness of the law for those who do not know the law. And how will He judge? "According to the gospel, through Christ" (Rom 2:16). Therefore both the gospel and Christ belong to the same God whose law and nature will be vindicated by that God through the gospel and Christ in the judgment spoken of above: "according to truth."

Just as the wrath revealed from heaven can come only from the God of wrath, so this interpretation, cohering with the earlier one in which the Creator's judgment is proclaimed, cannot be transferred to another God who neither judges nor grows angry, but must belong to the One whose judgment and wrath these are, and necessarily also the gospel and Christ, through whom these transactions take place.

That is why he launches an attack on transgressors of the law who teach "do not steal" yet steal — acting as a man of God's law, not as the Creator Himself being touched in these ways, since the One who forbade stealing commanded fraud against the Egyptians for gold and silver, just as other passages are twisted against Him. Clearly the apostle feared to make a public reproach against the God from whom he did not fear to turn away. Yet he pressed the Jews so hard that he inserted a prophetic rebuke: "Because of you the name of God is blasphemed" (Rom 2:24). How perverse, then, that he himself would blaspheme the very One whose blasphemy he denounces in the wicked!

He also prefers circumcision of the heart to circumcision of the flesh. But with God circumcision of the heart, not the flesh, has been effected — by the Spirit, not the letter. If this is the circumcision of Jeremiah — "Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts" (Jer 4:4) — and of Moses — "Circumcise your hardened hearts" (Deut 10:16) — then the Spirit who circumcises the heart belongs to the same God whose letter cuts the flesh, and whose Jew is both the hidden one and the open one, because the apostle would not have named the Jew if he were not serving the God of the Jews.

"Once the law, now the justice of God through the faith of Christ" (Rom 3:21-22). What is this distinction? Did your God serve the Creator's arrangement, giving Him time and His law? Or the One who was then and is now? Whose law, and whose faith of Christ? The distinction is one of arrangements, not of gods. He warns those justified by the faith of Christ to have peace with God (Rom 5:1). With which God? The one whose enemies we never were, or the one whose law and nature we rebelled against? For if peace is offered to the One with whom there was war, we will be justified to Him; and Christ will be His, through whose faith we are justified, to whose peace it belongs that His enemies be subdued.

"The law entered so that the trespass might abound" (Rom 5:20). Why? "So that grace might abound all the more" (Rom 5:20). Whose God's grace, if not the One whose law it also is? Unless the Creator inserted the law to procure an occasion for the grace of another God — and a rival at that, not to say an unknown one — so that just as sin reigned in death, so grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ (Rom 5:21) with His own adversary. For this reason the Creator's law shut up everything under sin and brought the whole world under guilt and stopped every mouth, so that no one might boast through it, so that grace might be preserved for the glory of Christ — not the Creator's Christ, but Marcion's!

I can even establish the substance of Christ here from the prospect of the coming question. For he says: "We have died to the law through the body of Christ" (Rom 7:4). Therefore Christ has a body. One may dispute whether it is a body, not immediately flesh! But whatever its substance, since he calls it a body and subjects it to having risen from the dead, no other body can be understood than one of flesh, in which the law of death is spoken. Yet he also bears witness to the law and excuses its cause: "What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means!" (Rom 7:7). I abhor it, Marcion — by no means! — the apostle abominating the accusation against the law: "I would not have known sin except through the law" (Rom 7:7). O supreme praise of the law, that through it sin was not allowed to hide! Therefore it is not the law that deceived, but sin through the occasion of the commandment. What do you impute to God's law, which the apostle dare not impute? And yet he piles on: "The law is holy, and the commandment is just and good" (Rom 7:12). If he venerates the Creator's law in this way, I do not know how he destroys it. Who distinguishes two gods, one just and the other good, when one must believe that the commandment of the one God is both good and just? But if he also confirms the spiritual law, then certainly the prophetic, certainly the figurative. I must therefore establish Christ as having been prefigured in the law, so that He could be recognized by all the Jews.
notes: The translation aims to follow the Latin text as closely as possible, while still being readable in English.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the nuances of Tertullian's polemic. All scripture citations in Pass B (Rom 1:16-17, Rom 2:2, Rom 2:16, Rom 2:24, Jer 4:4, Deut 10:16, Rom 3:21-22, Rom 5:1, Rom 5:20, Rom 5:21, Rom 7:4, Rom 7:7, Rom 7:12) correctly identify the verses alluded to in the Latin. The distinction between 'disposition' (dispositionis) and 'gods' (deorum) is maintained. The translation of 'opusculum profligatur' as 'pamphlet is being dismantled' and 'tramittenda' as 'pass over' is faithful to the sense.
